extracted.intended_audience: scientists, philosophers, and students studying the philosophy and method of scientific inquiry
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating and constructing scientific theories: how to discover laws (induction), deduce consequences (ratiocination), and test them (verification), and how to explain laws by resolving them into more general laws or constituents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deductive Method — Induction, Ratiocination, Verification
rubrics_metrics.description: The Deductive Method is characterized by three constituent parts: Induction, Ratiocination, and Verification; to be reliable, deductive conclusions must be verified by observation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All three parts are essential; without Verification the results of deduction have little other value than conjecture. The Deductive Method enables large phenomena to be embraced under simple laws, but its conclusions must be compared with direct experience where obtainable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Induction / Method of Agreement
rubrics_metrics.description: Ascertain empirical laws of the effect by comparison of instances, conformably to the Method of Agreement, and describe phenomena in the most comprehensive and accurate manner possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect observations and express from parts the simplest correct expressions for corresponding wholes (e.g., express observed planetary places first by a circle, then by epicycles, then by an ellipse). As many empirical laws as possible should be ascertained to facilitate verification and theory-building.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ratiocination / Deductive reasoning from general law to particular cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Reasoning from a general law to a particular case: determining by means of the particular circumstances of that case what result is required to fulfill the law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ratiocination can be used to discover a law or to explain a law already discovered (e.g., Torricellian experiment: from general equilibrium and knowledge that air has weight one can deduce mercury column height). Deduction requires knowledge of the relevant causes and their relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verification — empirical test of deductive conclusions
rubrics_metrics.description: Verification is the test by which we judge whether errors in deduction (such as omitted causes or inaccurate laws) have been committed; conclusions must accord with results of direct observation wherever it can be had.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If deductions predict a given effect from a combination of causes, then in all known cases where that combination existed and the effect did not follow, one must show (or plausibly surmise) what frustrated it. Verification is not complete unless some confirming cases are of at least equal complexity to those in which the theory will be applied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theory must deductively imply known empirical laws
rubrics_metrics.description: When empirical laws of the effect exist, the most effectual verification of a theory is that it leads deductively to those empirical laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A satisfactory theory should account for observed uniformities (complete or incomplete). Example: it was deemed essential that any true theory of celestial causes should lead to Kepler’s laws; use known empirical laws as tests of proposed explanations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of complex instances for verification
rubrics_metrics.description: Complex cases that were of no use for discovery may nevertheless verify an analysis and become additional evidence of the laws themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such cases serve as new trials of the principle in different circumstances and can help eliminate previously unexcluded circumstances (example: discrepancy in sound velocity explained by heat released during compression). Thus complex instances can increase certainty of a law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explanation by resolution into separate causes (composition of causes)
rubrics_metrics.description: A law of a complex effect is explained when it is resolved into the separate laws of the causes which contribute to it, together with the fact of their co-existence (collocations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To explain the law of a combined effect one must state the simpler laws of the tendencies and the collocation (existence and relative amounts) of the agents—e.g., planetary motion resolved into rectilineal inertia and centripetal gravitation. Collocations are as essential as the simpler laws themselves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explanation by intermediate links (mediating phenomena)
rubrics_metrics.description: A law connecting two non-proximate links may be explained by detecting an intermediate link (A → B → C), so that the original A→C relation is resolved into A→B and B→C.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When an intermediate phenomenon B is shown to mediate, the laws connecting A with B and B with C are more general than A→C and are less liable to error; examples include nerve changes mediating touch and sensation, or chemical decomposition mediating acid corrosion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explanation by subsumption under a more general law (unification)
rubrics_metrics.description: Several particular laws may be gathered into one more general law that includes them all; the general law is formed by combining partial laws observed under different conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This process (subsumption/unification) produces the most general laws by successive steps (e.g., unifying terrestrial gravity and celestial central force under universal gravitation, or affiliating magnetism under laws of electricity). The general law is the sum of the partial ones and requires distinct sets of observations to establish.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference for more general and more certain laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Laws resolved into other laws are typically resolved into laws more general and more to be relied on; such laws are nearer to universal truth and are defeated by fewer contingencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: More general (elementary) laws hold in more cases and are less likely to require limitation by subsequent experience; therefore, in explanation and theory choice, prefer laws that extend over more cases and are less conditional.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complex laws are less general and more liable to failure
rubrics_metrics.description: The law of a complex effect is inherently less general than the laws of its separate causes and is subject to all the negative conditions that may defeat any of those causes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A complex law may fail because any contingency that defeats any contributing cause defeats the joint effect (example: rusting of a small part of a machine may prevent its operation). Also, varying proportions of the same causes may produce qualitatively different results (e.g., different conic sections from different force ratios).

rubrics_metrics.name: Explanation means pointing to more general laws and collocations (not asserting a new 'cause')
rubrics_metrics.description: To explain a law of nature is to point out other, more general laws and the collocations under which the partial law is a case; explanation substitutes a more general phenomenon or law for a less general one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is not to assert that the general law 'causes' the partial one in the everyday sense; rather, the partial law is a case of the general one. 'Accounting for' a law means showing it follows from more general laws plus collocations, enabling deduction of its conditions.
